article.title: GrapheneOS Defends Its Duress-Wipe Feature After Federal Prosecutors Charge Atlanta Activist Over a Wiped Pixel Phone
article.summary: GrapheneOS publicly defended its security model after federal prosecutors charged an Atlanta activist over a Pixel phone that went blank during a CBP airport search.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Federal prosecutors are pursuing criminal charges against Atlanta resident Sam Tunick after his Google Pixel phone, running the privacy-focused GrapheneOS operating system, went blank and lost its contents during a search at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport — a case that has now drawn a direct public response from the GrapheneOS project itself, according to [CyberInsider](https://cyberinsider.com/grapheneos-defends-security-model-after-us-prosecutors-target-user/). CyberInsider reports that "federal prosecutors are now attempting to charge him under a federal law that prohibits destroying property to prevent it from being seized by authorities," after "agents repeatedly asked Tunick to unlock his Google Pixel phone" and, once he entered his passcode, "the device's screen went blank, restarted, and its contents were no longer accessible."

## What We Know

- Tunick was stopped for interrogation at Hartsfield-Jackson airport on January 24, 2025, after returning from a vacation in the Dominican Republic, according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone). The stop involved a Customs and Border Patrol tactical terrorism response team and an FBI Atlanta joint-terrorism task force officer, and federal authorities had put him on a terrorism watchlist beforehand, the Guardian reports.
- Court records reviewed by Cybernews read: "On or about January 24th, 2025, in the Northern District of Georgia," matching the date reported by the Guardian, according to [Cybernews](https://cybernews.com/privacy/atlanta-man-border-search-prosecuted-grapheneos/).
- During questioning, Tunick "asked four times ... to speak with a lawyer, but was rebuffed each time, according to courtroom testimony," and "the agents produced no warrant and did not read Tunick his rights," according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone). CBP officer Larry Findley told the court that agents were "looking for anything that's prohibited," the Guardian reports.
- Prosecutors are pursuing the case under a little-known federal statute that makes it a crime to destroy property to prevent its seizure — a statute The Guardian links to 18 U.S.C. § 2232 — in a case that had its first hearing this past Monday, according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone). Cybernews independently describes the same statute as one that "makes it illegal to destroy property in an effort to prevent it from being seized," according to [Cybernews](https://cybernews.com/privacy/atlanta-man-border-search-prosecuted-grapheneos/).
- Supporters connect the case to opposition against the "Cop City" police training center. Marlon Kautz, a member of the Atlanta Solidarity Fund, said: "We all have a right to secure our private data against unconstitutional searches. And we should – especially in a time of rising authoritarianism," according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone). The Guardian describes Cop City as "the $109m police training center, which opened last spring."
- Cybersecurity and surveillance expert Christophe Boutry called the prosecution "concerning – and sends the message that [GrapheneOS] is criminal by default." He separately said: "The main goal [of the operating system] is protection of privacy. They're our phones and the state can't tell us how to use them," according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone). Boutry and Bill Buddington, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, both told the Guardian they had not seen a similar case before.
- The Electronic Frontier Foundation has separately argued: "A person's privacy interests in the personal data on a phone or laptop are extraordinarily different from their limited privacy interests in the contents of their suitcase," according to [Cybernews](https://cybernews.com/privacy/atlanta-man-border-search-prosecuted-grapheneos/).
- In response to the Guardian's report, GrapheneOS published a statement defending its security architecture, according to [CyberInsider](https://cyberinsider.com/grapheneos-defends-security-model-after-us-prosecutors-target-user/). The project said "GrapheneOS has strong defenses against data extraction," built on "the standard security features provided by Android 17 and the most secure hardware available for Android," and clarified that its optional duress PIN/password feature — which "securely wipes a device when entered" — "is only one component of its broader security model and is not required to protect user data from extraction."
- A judge's decision on Tunick's motion to suppress evidence "will take at least until end of October," according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone).

## What We Don't Know

- Public reporting has not resolved whether Tunick deliberately triggered a preset duress code or whether the wipe followed his entry of a regular passcode. The Guardian's account describes agents demanding he unlock the phone and the screen going "blank, flashed several times and the phone appeared to restart" after he provided a passcode, without specifying intent — even as GrapheneOS and Cybernews frame the episode around the operating system's duress feature specifically.
- Neither outlet has published the case's docket number, and no ruling date beyond "end of October" has been reported.

## Analysis

The case tests, for what both a cybersecurity expert and an EFF technologist told the Guardian is unprecedented territory, whether using a privacy tool exactly as designed can itself be treated as evidence destruction. GrapheneOS's decision to publicly re-explain that its duress-wipe feature is optional and secondary to its broader encryption and hardware protections, according to [CyberInsider](https://cyberinsider.com/grapheneos-defends-security-model-after-us-prosecutors-target-user/), suggests the project is trying to avoid the narrative — voiced by Boutry — that running privacy-hardened software is "criminal by default," according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone).
